question: Explain the CSS box model and the difference between content-box and border-box sizing.

key_points: The box model: content, padding, border, margin — each layer wraps around the previous one
content-box (default): width/height apply only to the content area; padding and border are added on top, making the total rendered size larger than the specified width
border-box: width/height include content, padding, and border — the specified width IS the final rendered size, with content shrinking to fit
Explains why border-box is generally preferred/commonly set globally (`* { box-sizing: border-box }`) since it makes sizing calculations much more predictable
reference_solution.sample_answer: The CSS box model describes an element as nested boxes: content in the center, then padding around it, then a border around that, then margin outside the border. With the default content-box sizing, the width and height you set apply only to the content area, and padding and border get added on top of that, so the actual rendered size ends up larger than the width you specified. With border-box sizing, the width and height instead include the content, padding, and border all together, so the value you set IS the final rendered size, and the content area just shrinks to accommodate the padding and border. Because content-box makes sizing calculations unintuitive — adding padding changes the total rendered size unexpectedly — most projects globally set box-sizing: border-box on everything, since it makes layout math far more predictable.

follow_up_hint: Ask them what happens to a fixed-width element's content area if you add padding without box-sizing: border-box set.

question: Explain how Flexbox's main-axis and cross-axis alignment properties work.

key_points: flex-direction determines the main axis (row = horizontal, column = vertical); the cross axis is perpendicular to it
justify-content aligns items along the main axis (space-between, center, flex-start/end, etc.)
align-items aligns items along the cross axis for a single line; align-content aligns multiple lines/rows of wrapped flex items along the cross axis
Explains this differs from Grid, which handles two dimensions natively rather than a single primary axis with a perpendicular cross-axis
reference_solution.sample_answer: In Flexbox, flex-direction determines which axis is the 'main axis' — row makes it horizontal, column makes it vertical — and the cross axis is always perpendicular to whichever the main axis is. justify-content controls alignment and spacing of items along the main axis, with values like center, space-between, or flex-start. align-items controls alignment along the cross axis for items within a single line — so for a row-direction flex container, align-items controls vertical alignment. If items wrap onto multiple lines, align-content additionally controls how those multiple lines are distributed along the cross axis, similar to how justify-content works for the main axis but for whole lines instead of individual items. This is a bit different conceptually from CSS Grid, which manages both dimensions natively as rows and columns, rather than thinking in terms of one primary axis and a perpendicular cross axis.

follow_up_hint: Ask them the difference between align-items and align-content, and when align-content actually has a visible effect.

question: What is CSS specificity, and how is it calculated when multiple rules apply to the same element?

key_points: Specificity determines which CSS rule 'wins' when multiple conflicting rules target the same element and property

Roughly calculated as a tuple/score: inline styles > ID selectors > class/attribute/pseudo-class selectors > element/pseudo-element selectors, compared in that priority order (not simply added as a single number)
!important overrides normal specificity rules entirely (highest priority short of browser user-agent overrides), and should be used sparingly since it makes overriding styles later much harder
When specificity is equal, the rule that appears later in the source order (or is loaded later) wins
reference_solution.sample_answer: Specificity determines which CSS rule takes precedence when multiple rules with conflicting values target the same element and property. It's calculated as a sort of tiered score, roughly: inline styles beat ID selectors, which beat class, attribute, and pseudo-class selectors, which beat plain element and pseudo-element selectors — and these tiers are compared in that priority order, not just summed into one flat number, so ten class selectors still lose to a single ID selector. The !important flag overrides normal specificity comparison almost entirely, so it should be used very sparingly, since once something is marked !important, overriding it later requires either another !important or came from a source of even higher priority, which quickly becomes hard to maintain. When two rules have exactly equal specificity, the one that appears later in the source, or that's loaded later, wins.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to compare the specificity of `.btn.primary` versus `#submit-button` and explain which wins.
